extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (or advanced undergraduates) studying algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises, definitions, and theorems about intersection numbers on algebraic surfaces, the Picard group and intersection form, criteria for ampleness/nefness (Nakai–Moishezon, Kleiman), and related constructions (Grothendieck group, Kähler differentials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection number — degree description
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition (20.2.0.1): intersection number given as deg_C O_X(D)|_C (the degree on C of the restriction of O_X(D)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as one of four equivalent descriptions of the intersection number; noted that this definition is not obviously symmetric in C and D. Used in computations and has geometric interpretation via line bundle restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection number — Euler characteristic description
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition (20.2.0.2): intersection number described via Euler characteristics (χ) — an algebraic/cohomological description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as "remarkably useful" (for exercises), but with the geometric picture somewhat obscured. Useful for computations involving Riemann–Roch and asymptotic arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection number — scheme-theoretic local length (h^0) description
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition (20.2.0.4): intersection number given by h^0 of the scheme-theoretic intersection (local, pointwise vector-space interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This description is clearly local: at each point of C ∩ D one has a vector space. Example: in A^2_k, y−x^2 meets the x-axis with multiplicity 2 because h^0(k[x,y]/(y−x^2,y)) has dimension 2. Also equal to the length of the dimension 0 scheme-theoretic intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection form on Pic(X)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Proposition 20.1.3, the intersection number induces a bilinear 'intersection form' Pic X × Pic X → Z (20.2.3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a bilinear pairing used throughout the section; Asymptotic Riemann–Roch implies χ(X,O(nD)) is a quadratic polynomial, reflecting the bilinearity/quadratic nature of intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: no topological moving lemma for curves with negative self-intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists an irreducible curve E with E^2 < 0, one cannot "move" E to an equivalent curve to compute self-intersection as in topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains an anti-pattern: moving lemmas from topology fail in algebraic geometry when negative self-intersection occurs; motivates careful intersection-theoretic definitions rather than relying on naive geometric movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjunction formula for curves on surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjunction formula (20.2.B(a)): For a (smooth) curve C on a smooth projective surface X, C·(K_X + C) = 2 p_a(C) − 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an exercise assuming Serre duality; other versions and hints are given (reference to other exercises). Essential for computing arithmetic genus from intersection data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Roch for surfaces (divisor form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Riemann–Roch for surfaces (20.2.B(b)): χ(X, O_X(D)) = (D·(D − K_X))/2 + χ(X, O_X) for any Weil divisor D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly (e.g., in ampleness arguments). Hinted connections to curve Riemann–Roch; used for asymptotic/cohomological computations of sections and Euler characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of (−1)-curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition (20.2.7): A curve C on a surface X is a (−1)-curve if C is isomorphic to P^1_k (consists of smooth points) and C^2 = −1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently can be phrased as 'C has normal bundle O(−1)'; exceptional divisors of blow-ups are (−1)-curves. This identifies a class of curves with predictable intersection behaviour and contraction properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodge Index Theorem for surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hodge Index Theorem (20.2.11): For an irreducible smooth projective surface X with H^2 > 0 and L·H = 0 (H ∈ Pic X ample), one has L^2 ≤ 0; equality holds iff L is numerically trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains signature behaviour of the intersection pairing on N^1(X) and the intuition of one positive direction coming from an ample class. Exercises and reductions (use of Serre duality, asymptotic arguments) are provided in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nakai–Moishezon criterion for ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem (20.4.1): If L is an invertible sheaf on a projective k-scheme X and for every subvariety Y of X of dimension n we have (L^n·Y) > 0, then L is ample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a characterization of ampleness by positivity on all subvarieties. Used as a tool in proofs (e.g., to deduce ampleness of perturbed line bundles) and in exercises; proof uses induction, asymptotic Riemann–Roch, and cohomological vanishing arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleiman's positivity theorem (nefness implies intersection nonnegativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kleiman's Theorem (20.4.6): If L is nef on a projective k-scheme X, then (L^k·V) ≥ 0 for every irreducible subvariety V ⊂ X of dimension k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key tool leading to Kleiman's numerical criterion; proof sketched by induction on dimension and via considering polynomials P(t) = (L + tH)^n with H very ample. Exercise consequences: limits of ample classes are nef, and nef+ample is ample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleiman's numerical criterion for ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem (20.4.7): (a) The nef cone is the closure of the ample cone. (b) The ample cone is the interior of the nef cone (for projective schemes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives numerical/topological description of ample vs. nef cones in N^1(X). Side remarks clarify differences in the proper (nonprojective) case and factorial hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampleness is a numerical property (depends only on class in N^1(X))
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark (20.4.2): (L^n·Y) depends only on the numerical equivalence class of L, so ampleness is determined numerically; the notion of ampleness makes sense on N^1(X)_Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because intersection numbers depend only on numerical equivalence, one may analyze ampleness via cones in N^1(X)_Q; used to argue openness of the ample cone and to perturb classes by small amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist/strategy to prove a line bundle is ample (proof outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof steps for Nakai–Moishezon (20.4.5): reduce to integral X, use Asymptotic Riemann–Roch to show large powers have sections; use exact sequences and vanishing to show sufficiently large powers are base-point-free on complements of divisors; deduce globally generated (or base-point-free) and positive degree on curves implies ampleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful procedural guidance: (1) show H^i vanish for large powers (Serre vanishing/induction), (2) get global sections for high powers, (3) control base locus via restriction to divisors and cohomology, (4) conclude ampleness using positivity on curves (Exercise 18.4.L). This gives a practical method to verify ampleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grothendieck group K(X) of coherent sheaves and its basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition (20.3.1): K(X) (often K_0(X)) is the abelian group generated by symbols [F] for coherent sheaves F subject to relations [F]=[F'] if isomorphic and [F']+[F'']=[F] for short exact sequences 0→F'→F→F''→0. If X is proper, χ descends to χ:K(X)→Z, and for integral X rank descends to rank:K(X)→Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: K(X) is filtered by dimension of support; the graded pieces A'_d(X) behave like homology groups; pushforwards and pullbacks (for proper/flat maps) are defined via higher direct images and exactness respectively. This is groundwork for algebraic homology-like theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action of first Chern class on K(X) (c1 operator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition (20.3.4): For an invertible sheaf L on X, define an operator L⊗ : K(X) → K(X) by [F] ↦ [L⊗F]. The induced map on graded pieces gives c1(L)∩ : A'_d(X) → A'_{d−1}(X), i.e., the action of the first Chern class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises show this operation is well-defined on the associated graded and additive after passing to A'_•(X). This recovers intersection products (L1·...·Ln·[F]) via iterated c1 actions on K-classes and connects the construction to Chow groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of A'_d(X) to Chow groups and (co)homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement (20.3.4.2): There is a surjective map A_d(X) → A'_d(X) (Chow groups → K-theory graded pieces), and this is an isomorphism after tensoring with Q. If k = C and X proper, A'_d(X) maps to H_{2d}(X,Q) (or Borel–Moore homology if X nonproper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that A'_d(X) approximate Chow groups, and over Q they coincide; highlights functoriality and compatibility with pushforwards and Chern class actions. Side remark: the kernel can have torsion in pathological cases (SGA6 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective and nef cone descriptions for Hirzebruch surfaces F_n
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises (20.2.I–20.2.S): For Fn = Proj_{P1}(O ⊕ O(n)), Pic Fn is generated by E (section of self-intersection −n) and F (fiber). Every effective curve on Fn is a non-negative combination of E and F; the nef cone is generated by C and F (or ℓ and m in special cases); Pic Fn ≅ Z E ⊕ Z F and intersection matrix computed accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These give concrete criteria for identifying effective and nef cones on ruled/Hirzebruch surfaces, and provide methods (local charts, intersection computations, use of moving families) for verifying generation and cone structure. Exercises show Fn are pairwise nonisomorphic via cone and intersection comparisons.
